questions.q: In a client-server interaction, which entity initiates the communication and which entity waits passively for a request? Give one real-world example naming the client and the server explicitly.
questions.a: The client initiates the communication; the server waits passively (listens) for incoming requests. Example: When you use the Gmail app on your phone to check email, the Gmail app is the client and Google's mail server is the server. A wrong answer (e.g., "server initiates") reveals the student thinks servers push data automatically like a broadcast, confusing client-server with push notifications or peer-to-peer where either node can start.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why a web browser is called a "thin client" in the context of client-server architecture, and give one situation where a "thick client" would be used instead.
questions.a: A thin client (like a browser) relies almost entirely on the server for processing and storage; it only handles display and user input. A thick client (like a desktop video editor or a game installed on your PC) does significant processing locally and only contacts the server for specific data (e.g., license verification, multiplayer sync). A wrong answer that says "thin client means small screen size" or "thick client means heavy software" shows confusion between hardware form-factor and architectural role.

questions.q: A school uses a central file server. Teachers save lesson plans on it from their laptops; students open read-only copies from the computer lab. Identify the client(s) and server in this scenario. If the file server crashes at 10 AM, what happens to (a) a teacher trying to save a new file at 10:05 AM, and (b) a student who already opened a file at 9:55 AM? Justify.
questions.a: Clients: teachers' laptops and lab computers (they request file save/open). Server: central file server (provides storage service). (a) Teacher's save request fails—server is down, so no response. (b) Student's already-opened file may still be accessible locally (cached in RAM), but any further save or new open will fail. A wrong answer claiming the student loses the open file immediately reveals misunderstanding of client-side caching vs. server dependency.

questions.q: Compare client-server and peer-to-peer (P2P) architectures on these three parameters: (i) centralised control, (ii) scalability as number of users grows, (iii) fault tolerance when one node fails. Use a table or bullet points.
questions.a: (i) Centralised control: Client-server has it (server manages access, authentication, data consistency); P2P has none (each peer is equal). (ii) Scalability: Client-server degrades—server becomes bottleneck; P2P scales better—each new peer adds capacity. (iii) Fault tolerance: Client-server has single point of failure (server down = service down); P2P is resilient (other peers continue). A wrong answer that says "P2P has centralised control" or "client-server scales infinitely" shows the student hasn't grasped the architectural trade-offs.

questions.q: A startup chooses client-server architecture for their new food-delivery app instead of P2P. Evaluate this decision: list two advantages and one disadvantage they will face, specifically in the context of handling 10,000 simultaneous orders during a festival peak.
questions.a: Advantages: (1) Centralised order management—easy to track, assign delivery partners, apply surge pricing uniformly. (2) Data consistency—single source of truth for restaurant menus, user addresses, payment status. Disadvantage: (3) Server bottleneck—10,000 concurrent requests may overwhelm a single server; they must invest in load balancing or cloud auto-scaling (which adds cost/complexity). A wrong answer focusing only on "easy to set up" without addressing the peak-load risk shows superficial evaluation.

questions.q: Design a simple client-server interaction for a "Digital Library" system where students can search book titles and reserve a copy. Draw a labelled diagram (text description acceptable) showing the client, server, network, and the sequence of messages for a successful reservation. Include at least three distinct message types (e.g., SEARCH_REQUEST, SEARCH_RESULT, RESERVE_REQUEST, RESERVE_CONFIRMATION).
questions.a:
Expected answer (text diagram):
```
[Student Laptop - CLIENT]                    [Library Server - SERVER]
       |                                          |
       |--- SEARCH_REQUEST("Python") ----------->|
       |<-- SEARCH_RESULT([BookID:101, "Python Basics"]) --|
       |                                          |
       |--- RESERVE_REQUEST(BookID:101, StudentID:S202) -->|
       |<-- RESERVE_CONFIRMATION(ReservationID:R555) ------|
       |                                          |
```
A poor answer that merges client and server into one box, omits the network, or uses only one message type reveals the student cannot decompose the interaction into discrete request-response steps.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Client-Server ______ is a distributed computing model where tasks are partitioned between service requesters (clients) and service providers (servers); clients initiate requests for resources or services, and servers listen for, process, and respond to those requests over a network.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you open a ______ on your phone and type "www.irctc.co.in" to book a train ticket.
What is Client-Server Architecture? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Client-Server Architecture is a distributed computing model where tasks are partitioned between service requesters (clients) and service providers (servers); clients initiate requests for resources or services, and servers listen for, process, and respond to those requests over a network.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Client-Server Architecture?
questions.a: Students often think "client" and "server" refer to specific hardware (e.g., "a server is a big rack-mounted machine, a client is a laptop").

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) distinguish client and server roles in a given real-world scenario (e.g., web browsing, email, database access) and explain the request-response cycle; (2) compare client-server with peer-to-peer architecture on at least three parameters (control, scalability, fault tolerance) with justification.
